title: Diagram Recall and Route Notation
researchQuestion: Which simple notation styles make branching routes in abstract diagrams easier to recall after a short viewing interval?
summary: This browser-based methods study compares line weight, node labels, and turn notation in invented floor-plan diagrams. It does not use real buildings, travel history, clinical measures, or location data. Enrollment is paused while the current protocol presentation is reviewed.
commitment: One session of approximately twelve minutes
eligibility: Access to a desktop, laptop, or tablet with a keyboard or pointing device.
Able to complete one uninterrupted twelve-minute session.
Able to read the study interface in English.
exclusions: No real building, route, workplace, residence, or travel information is used.
No medical history, diagnosis, vision record, cognitive assessment, webcam, microphone, or eye tracking is requested.
participantActivities: Review a short sequence of abstract branching diagrams built from neutral lines, nodes, and symbols.
After each viewing interval, select the route sequence that matches the displayed diagram.
Complete a fixed-choice comparison of notation clarity and input method.

protocolSteps.title: Orient
protocolSteps.description: Review the task key and practice with one diagram excluded from the study sequence.

protocolSteps.title: View
protocolSteps.description: Inspect an abstract branching diagram for the assigned fixed interval.

protocolSteps.title: Recall
protocolSteps.description: Select the matching route from fixed alternatives after the diagram closes.

protocolSteps.title: Compare
protocolSteps.description: Rate the clarity of the notation using a short fixed-choice scale.

dataRequested: Selected route alternative for each abstract diagram.
Optional prior familiarity category for diagram or map use.
dataNotRequested: Real routes, addresses, building plans, location history, or travel records.
Name, contact information, medical history, diagnosis, or accessibility records.
Camera, microphone, eye tracking, biometric input, or device fingerprinting.
samplePrompts: Which route sequence matches the diagram shown immediately before this screen?
Which node-label style was easiest to distinguish?
Was the task completed with a keyboard, pointing device, or touch input?
methodNotes: Every diagram is invented for the protocol and uses the same number of nodes and route branches within its comparison set.
Viewing intervals and response choices are fixed before each task sequence.
The activity measures task responses only and is not presented as an evaluation of individual ability.
limitations: Screen size, viewing distance, ambient light, and input method vary between remote sessions.
A short abstract task does not establish performance in real navigation or emergency wayfinding.
The current pause concerns protocol presentation and does not imply a finding.
